why: Each character of the new password may match itself or its cyclic successor, and the old password must be a subsequence. That is the standard greedy subsequence check with two pointers, where 'equal' is widened to 'equal or one step ahead'.
hints: Each index of the new password is changed at most once and only by +1. So what letters can position j stand for?
new[j] can play c if c == new[j] or c == next(new[j]). With that matching rule, check whether old is a subsequence of new.
Two pointers: walk through new; advance the old pointer whenever the current new character can play old's current character. YES if old is fully matched. O(total length).
pitfalls: Taking the earliest possible match is always safe; no backtracking is needed.
A character cannot be shifted twice: 'a' can match 'a' or 'b', never 'c'.
constraints:
• 1 ≤ n ≤ 10
  • 1 ≤ oldPasswords[i].length ≤ newPasswords[i].length
  • Total length of all strings ≤ 2 * 10^5
  • Lowercase English letters only
